prompts.search:
You are a research agent for Community Notes fact-checking on X/Twitter.

Your job: investigate whether the post's main claim / argument is incorrect and would benefit from a community note. Use the web_search tool to find evidence.

## Output format
Return JSON with two fields:
- findings: a dense research summary. Include the full https:// source URL inline next to each claim it supports — write out the complete link, never use footnote numbers, domain shortcuts, or citation markers.
- correction_needed: true only if the post's main claim / argument is incorrect and would benefit from a community note.

## When NOT to set correction_needed = true
- The correction does not address the main claim / argument of the post
- Opinions, satire, jokes, hyperbole
- Posts that are factually correct
- When you can't find strong contradicting evidence
- When the "error" is too minor or pedantic

## Sourcing rules
- Tweets and tweet replies from the comments are valid sources and can be included in the findings (include full x.com URL).
- Include what each source says that's relevant.
- If no correction is needed, the findings can be brief — just explain why.

Respond with strict JSON only matching: { findings: string, correction_needed: boolean }
prompts.writer:
You are a Community Notes writer for X/Twitter. You receive the original post context and research findings from a prior search step. Your job: write exactly one community note that disputes a specific factual claim in the post — or return an empty note if you cannot find one to dispute.

## The one rule

**Your note must DISPUTE something the tweet asserts.** If the research findings do not contain evidence that contradicts a specific claim in the tweet, return an empty note — do NOT write a note that:
- Restates the tweet's claim in different words
- Adds adjacent context that doesn't contradict anything (e.g. tweet says X happened, you say X was later partially reversed — that's not a dispute)
- Cites a source that *agrees* with the tweet as if you're correcting it
- Asserts specifics (locations, dates, who-said-what, URLs) that don't appear verbatim in the findings — never fabricate

Empty note means: `note_text` = "" and `sources` = []. The downstream judge will record "no_correction_needed" and we move on. This is correct behavior when no evidence-supported dispute is available.

## Note style
- Lead with what IS true, not "The post claims..." or "This is false"
  GOOD: "This video was recorded in January 2024 during a murder trial."
  BAD: "The post falsely claims that..."
- One key fact. Pick the single strongest piece of evidence that relates to the thing you are writing about.
- 1-2 sentences before the URL. Short and direct. Notes regularly get approved with a single sentence asserting the true state of affairs.
- No hedging: don't say "appears to", "seems to", "potentially"
- Neutral, bridging tone: people who agree AND disagree with the post should both find it fair
- No sarcasm, no "gotcha" framing, no partisan language
- Prefer primary sources (official sites, X posts, Wikipedia, YouTube originals) over news articles

## Character limit
- Limit: 240-260 non-URL characters. Shorter is fine
- Hard max: 280 non-URL characters (URLs are shortened by X and count as 1 character each)
- Be concise. Every word must earn its place.

## Source rules
- Every source must DIRECTLY support your specific correction (not just general background)
- Don't add redundant sources
- Tweets or tweet replies can be valid sources, but are worse than generic ones, eg wikipedia, a trusted centrist news site.
- Pull source URLs from the research findings — do not invent URLs

## What the checker will do
A checker splits your note into its separate factual claims and rejects the whole note if any one claim is not stated by a source you cite. So:
- Every sentence must be backed by one of your cited URLs. A fact that is in the findings but not in a URL you cite gets the note rejected: cite the URL it came from, or leave the fact out.
- Make one or two claims. Every extra detail (a date, a name, a second correction, background) is another claim that needs a source and another reason for a rater to reject.
- Never assert that something did not happen, does not exist, or has no record ("no evidence", "no reports", "never", "still exists") unless a cited source says so in as many words. Say what is true instead.
prompts.timing:
You read an X post and research findings about it, and answer one narrow question: WHEN did the event the post describes happen?

Return JSON:
- event_time_utc: string | null — your best estimate of when the event happened, as an ISO 8601 UTC timestamp (e.g. "2026-08-05T14:30:00Z"). Precision to the hour is fine. null when the post is not about a datable event (evergreen claims, old photos resurfacing, general statistics).
- why: one short sentence.

Date the EVENT, not the post: an old video reposted today is an old event. A post claiming a death, score, transfer, or ruling that had reportedly just happened is a recent event even if the claim is false — date what the claim is about. For a claim about a still-developing situation (an ongoing search, a running count, a match in progress), the event is the latest development the claim rests on. Use dates in the findings and the post itself; do not compute any durations — just name the time.

result.findings:
Two separate claims need checking here.

1) The main rebuttal is broadly fair. D'Souza is answering a post that says 'virtually every place in India where Indians live' looks like a garbage-choked drainage channel. That sweeping claim is hyperbole. The quoted post offers no evidence for it, and saying 'most of India never looked like this' is a reasonable opinion. That part doesn't need a note.

2) The supporting claim that 'the slums that I saw as a kid in Mumbai are largely gone now' is contradicted by the evidence. The tagging user's point about Dharavi holds up.
- Dharavi still exists. It is 'often considered one of the world's largest slums,' with an estimated 700,000 to 1,000,000 residents on about 2.39 sq km (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dharavi).
- A 2023 academic paper says Dharavi is expected to reach about one million people by 2030. It also notes that Mumbai had the second-highest share of slum residents among India's million-plus cities, 41.8% in the 2011 Census (https://ic-sd.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/2023-submission_701.pdf).
- Redevelopment has barely started. The Adani-led Dharavi Redevelopment Project, approved in 2022, aims to rehouse more than 1 million slum dwellers. Its first phase only plans to hand over buildings by December 2026 and to start building 30,000 units in FY27 (https://www.newkerala.com/news/a/adani-groups-urban-project-mumbai-rehabilitate-over-million-171.htm).
- AFP photos from July 2025 still show densely packed slum homes in Dharavi (https://gulfnews.com/amp/story/world%2Fasia%2Findia%2Fasias-largest-slum-in-mumbai-to-undergo-8b-makeover-1.500295919).
- Earlier redevelopment plans going back to 2003-2004 repeatedly failed (https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2023/1/24/hopes-and-fears-as-slumdog-millionaire-slum-faces-wrecking-ball).
- Residents still resist the plans (https://vidhilegalpolicy.in/blog/redeveloping-slums-or-displacing-the-poor/).
- City officials have estimated that a large share of Mumbai's population lives in slums, on pavements or along railway tracks (https://archleague.org/article/rethinking-dharavi-an-analysis-of-redevelopment-programs-for-slums-in-mumbai-india/?printpage=true).

Conclusion: India has improved a lot since the 1970s, and the claim that all of India looks like the photo is an exaggeration. Still, the specific factual claim that Mumbai's slums are 'largely gone' is false. Mumbai's largest slums, Dharavi above all, are still home to around a million people, and redevelopment is only in its early stages. A note could add that context about the slum claim without disputing the broader point that not all of India looks like the photo.

The post's main point is that it isn't true that virtually every place in India where Indians live looks like the garbage-choked waterway in the quoted image. That is an obvious exaggeration in the quoted post, and rejecting it is a reasonable, mostly opinion-based argument. The claims about India improving since the 1970s and about modern hotels and airports are broad statements that are hard to note. One supporting line is wrong, though: the claim that the slums he saw as a kid in Mumbai are 'largely gone now.' The reader who tagged the bot is right that Dharavi still exists. Mumbai's largest slum covers about 2.1 sq km and is home to roughly 800,000 to 1,000,000 people, and other big Mumbai slums include Baiganwadi, Antop Hill, Sion-Koliwada, Worli-BDD Chawls and Malvani (https://www.nobroker.in/blog/slum-areas-in-mumbai/). A July 2026 source still calls Dharavi home to more than a million people living in dense informal settlements (https://lsfellowship.missouri.edu/article/dharavi-the-world-s-largest-slum-unveiled). Redevelopment has only just started. In June 2026 the Dharavi Redevelopment Project Authority told about 3,500 Sector 6 households to vacate. The first phase is 11,000 rehab homes on a timeline running to 2032, with the Adani Group, the Maharashtra government and the Slum Rehabilitation Authority behind it (https://www.propnewz.com/blog/dharavi-redevelopment-rehabilitation-mumbai-2026-06-28). The Supreme Court refused to halt the project (https://www.tribuneindia.com/news/india/sc-refuses-to-order-status-quo-on-adanis-dharavi-redevelopment-project/amp). So the line about Mumbai slums being 'largely gone' is false. But it is a side claim backing up an argument against an obvious generalization, and the post's main argument holds up. A note isn't clearly warranted. If one were written, it should be limited to the fact that Dharavi and other major Mumbai slums still exist and that redevelopment is in its early stages.

- AFP photos from July 2025 still show densely packed slum homes in Dharavi (https://gulfnews.com/amp/story/world%2Fasia%2Findia%2Fasias-largest-slum-in-mumbai-to-undergo-8b-makeover-1.500295919).
- Earlier redevelopment plans going back to 2003-2004 repeatedly failed (https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2023/1/24/hopes-and-fears-as-slumdog-millionaire-slum-faces-wrecking-ball).
- Residents still resist the plans (https://vidhilegalpolicy.in/blog/redeveloping-slums-or-displacing-the-poor/).
- City officials have estimated that a large share of Mumbai's population lives in slums, on pavements or along railway tracks (https://archleague.org/article/rethinking-dharavi-an-analysis-of-redevelopment-programs-for-slums-in-mumbai-india/?printpage=true).

Conclusion: India has improved a lot since the 1970s, and the claim that all of India looks like the photo is an exaggeration. Still, the specific factual claim that Mumbai's slums are 'largely gone' is false. Mumbai's largest slums, Dharavi above all, are still home to around a million people, and redevelopment is only in its early stages. A note could add that context about the slum claim without disputing the broader point that not all of India looks like the photo.

result.findings:
The claim the reader flagged checks out. The post's figures are accurate, so it doesn't need a note.

- **Share of world GDP.** The IMF's April 2026 World Economic Outlook puts US nominal GDP at about $32.38 trillion for 2026 (https://www.worldometers.info/gdp/us-gdp/). An aggregator using IMF data puts the US at $32.38T, or 25.9% of a roughly $125 trillion world economy (https://statisticsoftheworld.com/snapshot/2026). Another source gives about 25.58% (https://livegdp.com/united-states-gdp/). BusinessStats lists about 26% of world GDP and says the US produces 'roughly a quarter of global output with about 4 percent of its people' (https://businesstats.com/gdp-of-the-united-states/). So '26% of global nominal GDP with around 4% of the population' matches IMF-based data. The numbers fit together: about 340 million people out of about 8.2 billion is roughly 4.1%, and US GDP per capita is around $94,430 (https://www.worldometers.info/gdp/us-gdp/), far above the global average of about $15,289 (https://statisticsoftheworld.com/snapshot/2026).

- **Other claims.** I didn't search these separately. From general knowledge, both are broadly consistent with standard data. Among G20 members, the US ranks at or near the top for labor productivity; the countries that rank higher, such as Ireland and Luxembourg, aren't in the G20. US firms also make up roughly 60 or more of the top 100 companies by market value.

- **Opinion.** The rest of the post, crediting @POTUS and saying 'our best days are still ahead', is political opinion and can't be fact-checked.

The reader's suspicion that the 26%/4% figure is 'made up' is mistaken. The figure is correct.
